newsitem.title: JAPAN: OLYMPICS-DOWNHILL DISPUTE HITS CULTURAL IMPASSE.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-DOWNHILL DISPUTE HITS CULTURAL IMPASSE.

text.p: Sport looks like ending up the loser in a dialogue of the deaf over the alpine skiing downhill races at the Nagano Winter Olympics next February.
Ski racers fear the blue riband event of the Games would be turned into a virtual lottery if the present short course is not extended to a higher starting point.
But international ski authorities' efforts to raise the start to make the races true tests of speed and skill have failed to impress the Japanese organisers.
They have refused to budge a centimetre as the argument has headed straight down a cultural impasse of mutual misunderstanding.

It now looks certain that when France's Luc Alphand -- or his successor as premier men's downhiller -- steps into the start gate at the Nagano Olympics, he will do so at 1,680 metres above sea level, not at the higher elevation favoured by the International Ski Federation (FIS).

Olympic competitors will not be allowed to ski through the environmentally sensitive protected area on Mount Happoone where FIS wants the downhill to start, even though recreational skiers routinely use the area.
Nagano organisers said Japan's national park laws prohibit development of "an official ski area" in the protected area but do not restrict entry of public skiers.

Promises by the FIS that no construction will be needed, that the ground will not be touched and that only a tent fixed on snow will be used at the proposed 1,800-metre start leave Nagano organisers unmoved.
So does the FIS threat that the course in Hakuba, 50 kms west of Nagano, will never be awarded another men's World Cup downhill unless the start is raised for the Games.

"We don't want to contravene any kind of domestic Japanese law," said chief organiser Makoto Kobayashi. "If ordinary skiers want to go there, they can. But as an organising committee we can't. We would become known as the organising committee that destroys the environment."

To outsiders, the organisers' stance may seem illogical, if not hypocritical. Can 50 downhillers using the course for a few days really have more impact on the environment than recreational skiers using the area all season, year after year?

For the Japanese that is the wrong question to ask. Refusing to raise the start, they believe, demonstrates to the entire world their commitment to the Games' environmental principles, even if those principles are ignored at other times.

"The Olympics is a world event and it is an honour to have the race, so the more prestigious the Olympics, the more we have to respect the law," said Shigeharu Tayama, director of the environment and nature conservation division of the Nagano prefecture government.

Ski officials take a far more pragmatic approach. "The course will probably run one minute, 25 seconds, which would make it the shortest Olympic downhill in history," said David Pym, who will serve as FIS technical delegate at the race.
"There's the potential for 20 racers to finish within a second of each other. Skiing ability will not be the factor. Luck will be the factor."

University professor Matsuji Matsuda, who organised an Olympic environmental advisory committee before Nagano was awarded the Games in 1991, has dismissed FIS's offer to anchor a start tent in snow. "I think it's impossible," he said. "What if there's a strong wind?"

He claimed local people do not want the start at 1,800 metres, although he agreed that they have not been asked. He said those skiing in the protected area are outsiders from Tokyo, not Nagano residents.
"My personal opinion is that they should get rid of the chairlift and stop the skiers from using the area," he said, adding that such a change would be "a gift from the Olympics."
Nagano organisers said the chairlift was built to prevent hikers from disturbing the area's fragile flora and fauna, so removing it would appear counter-productive.
In contrast to Matsuda, they also said the main users were local skiers claiming a vested right to use the area, which was declared a protected zone in 1984, eight years after the lift was built.

Nagano organisers have further clouded the issue by insisting that permanent buildings are needed at the start for timing and television, that athletes would not tolerate starts from tents, and that a pond separating the two areas would require extensive earthworks to join.

Seiko, the official Games timer, ORTO, the organisation that produces the international television signal, and CBS, the American network that paid a record $375 million for U.S. broadcasting rights, have all said no permanent buildings are required.
Alpine racers routinely start from tents. The FIS has said that incorporating the pond would require no earthworks because it is frozen solid in winter.
Behind all the various arguments lurks the inevitable thought that the differences are more cultural than anything else.
"Western thinking is much more logical," said Saiki Terasawa, a university professor and mother of two. "Japanese are more spiritual.

"We see the Olympic Games as a symbol," she added. "The Games should play a leadership role. If the course is used for the Olympics, people will regard it as an official course and it will be used for other races. Once you use the course, once you have an example in Japan, you follow that. It sets up a precedent that is very difficult to change.
"We are afraid of that," she said.
